doc.title: Terri Lyne Carrington interviewed by Monk Rowe, Toronto, Canada, January 9, 2003

title: Trust and eye contact on the bandstand
summary: She discusses the trust and camaraderie needed to play creative jazz and how rhythm sections use eye contact.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: Great drummers: who they admired and why

blocks.x: When you play the creative jazz you’ve been speaking about, how important is it to like the people you’re playing with? I don’t know if “like” is the right word.

I know what you mean though. There is a certain kind of camaraderie that is important I believe when you are on stage with someone, because I think that you have to be able to trust in order to really be able to reach the highest musical marriage on stage, there is a certain amount of trust that is important. I have played with people whereas we didn’t necessarily hit it off offstage or maybe we just had some conflicts and maybe it was resolved. But still I’d give a hundred percent, and the other musicians that I know that’s good does the same, so the music would not really seem to suffer. But say I can’t look this person in the eye when I’m playing. You know? Until that real trust is there and you can look up and smile and look at each other, and I think that adds another level of intimacy.
Right. As opposed to just kind of turning your head and you’re still concentrating but it’s more of an ear thing.

Right. I mean it’s always an ear thing. I mean I don’t have to see anybody. It’s great to be able to see the leader especially because obviously there’s cues and little things that you may notice. That’s important. But as far as seeing all the musicians while they’re playing I mean the one player that stands out front, for the most part they don’t see anybody. So you don’t really have to see the person, but in the rhythm section sometimes eye contact is really great. So if you’re not really having the best relationship at the time with someone else in the rhythm section, you know it might be hard to look them in the eye and smile and cheer each other one. Though my experience has been that the music has not really suffered it just may not have the same kind of intimate factor that you would have when you can do that.
